s: W. R. Berkley Corp DEF 14A filed 22 April 2026 (ownership as of 9 April 2026); WRB close 68.60 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Proxy beneficial ownership table: 5,902,770 shares, 1.5 percent of class, held separately from his father William Berkley 23.3 percent block. 5,902,770 x 68.60 = 404.9 million dollars; rounded to 0.42 for deferred RSUs not in the table.
did: Joined his father specialty insurer W. R. Berkley in 1997, ran its international operations, became president in 2009 and chief executive in 2015, and grew net premiums past 12 billion dollars a year by launching new underwriting units rather than buying rivals; holds 1.5 percent of the company in his own name.
why: W. R. Berkley runs about 60 semi-autonomous underwriting units, each free to shrink when pricing turns soft, so the group compounds book value instead of chasing premium share. Officer pay is restricted stock deferred until retirement, so his stake compounds rather than being sold down.
obst: He took the chief executive seat in 2015 from the founder who was also his father, then spent the 2016 to 2019 soft commercial market cutting back lines and exiting business while peers grew premium, which meant defending flat revenue to shareholders for three straight years.
turn: The 2019 decision to lean into the hardening casualty market and reprice the book, which drove return on equity above 20 percent and roughly tripled the share price by 2026.

s: Interactive Brokers Group DEF 14A filed 11 March 2026 and Form 10-K filed 27 February 2026 (age 59); IBKR close 93.87 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Proxy ownership table: 2,730,868 shares (2,188,242 held plus 542,626 vesting), 0.61 percent of Class A. 2,730,868 x 93.87 = 256.3 million dollars. Proxy also attributes 5.64 million dollars of 2025 entity taxes to his retained IBG Holdings units, so rounded to 0.29.
did: Joined Interactive Brokers in 1990 as a software developer straight out of the Technical University of Budapest, wrote much of the order routing and risk code, became president in 2014 and chief executive in 2019, and now runs a broker with more than 4 million accounts and 60 billion dollars of equity capital.
why: Interactive Brokers automated work rivals staffed with people, so accounts grew roughly tenfold while headcount barely moved and pretax margin sat near 75 percent. The engineers who built that automation were paid in IBG Holdings units, so the code writers, not the salespeople, took the equity.
obst: The options market making arm that had funded the firm was being destroyed by penny quoting and high frequency competition through 2012 to 2017; he had to shut the market maker that was the company original business and bet everything on the lower margin brokerage.
turn: The 2017 exit from options market making, after which brokerage account growth compounded above 20 percent a year and the share price rose about eightfold.

s: Eagle Point Credit Company DEF 14A filed 6 April 2026 (age 51, managing partner and founder); Eagle Point platform assets under management of 14 billion dollars, firm disclosure 2026
m: Fee arithmetic on disclosed AUM: 14 billion dollars at a blended 1.2 percent management fee is about 170 million dollars of annual fee revenue before incentive fees; a 125 person cost base leaves roughly 70 to 80 million of annual profit, mostly his after the Stone Point minority, compounded since 2012.
did: Founded Eagle Point Credit Management in Greenwich in 2012 with seed backing from Stone Point Capital to buy the equity tranche of collateralized loan obligations, then took the strategy retail through listed closed end funds in 2014 and 2019, reaching 14 billion dollars of assets.
why: CLO equity is the residual tranche banks and insurers cannot hold, and sourcing it needs relationships with dozens of loan managers. Wrapping it in a listed fund paying monthly distributions turned a redeemable hedge fund trade into permanent capital, so fees keep accruing through drawdowns.
obst: In March and April 2020 loan prices gapped, CLO equity marks fell by more than half, and the listed fund breached asset coverage tests, forcing distribution cuts and deleveraging while retail holders sold; the vehicle he built to be permanent nearly failed its first stress test.
turn: The October 2014 listing of Eagle Point Credit Company, which turned an institutional carry trade into permanent public capital that could not be redeemed.

s: The Hartford Insurance Group DEF 14A filed 9 April 2026 (ownership as of 23 March 2026, age 65); HIG close 136.10 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Beneficial ownership 2,395,003 shares of which 1,937,189 are exercisable options. Shares: 457,814 x 136.10 = 62.3 million dollars. Options: proxy tables show strikes of 48.89 to 95.74 dollars, giving roughly 155 million dollars of intrinsic value, about 100 million after exercise tax.
did: Joined The Hartford as chief financial officer in 2010 while it was still repaying crisis era capital, became chief executive in 2014, sold the Japan annuity book and the Talcott run off life business, bought Navigators for 2.1 billion dollars in 2019, and rebuilt it as a small commercial property casualty underwriter.
why: The Hartford traded at a discount because a variable annuity book with tens of billions of guarantees sat behind a good property casualty franchise. Selling that tail removed the equity risk capping the multiple, and his pay was ten year options struck between 2015 and 2020, so the re-rating is the wealth.
obst: He inherited a company that had taken 3.4 billion dollars of TARP money and still carried variable annuity guarantees that could move billions with the equity market, then fought off an unsolicited 23 billion dollar approach from Chubb in 2020 while arguing the standalone plan was worth more.
turn: The May 2018 sale of Talcott Resolution, the run off annuity unit, which finally severed the 2008 legacy and let the company be valued as a pure property casualty underwriter.

s: The Cigna Group DEF 14A filed 13 March 2026 (ownership as of 30 January 2026, age 60); CI close 277.51 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Proxy: 1,204,028 shares beneficially owned including 342,814 options struck at 149.14 to 197.35 dollars. Shares 861,214 x 277.51 = 239 million dollars; option intrinsic about 34 million. Proxy separately states his holdings net of unvested stock equal 0.23 percent of a 73.3 billion dollar company.
did: Joined Cigna in 1991 as a financial analyst, became chief executive in 2009, and after regulators blocked the Anthem merger bought Express Scripts for 67 billion dollars in 2018, turning a mid sized health insurer into a pharmacy services company whose Evernorth unit now carries most of the profit.
why: Insurance margins are capped by medical loss ratio rules; pharmacy benefit management is not. Buying Express Scripts moved Cigna profit into rebate aggregation and specialty dispensing, which regulators do not cap, and his pay was overwhelmingly stock, so the shift compounded into his own holding.
obst: The 54 billion dollar Anthem merger he agreed in 2015 collapsed in 2017 in antitrust court and ended in litigation between the two buyers, leaving Cigna subscale and openly discussed as a takeover target; he had roughly a year to find an alternative before someone bought him.
turn: March 2018, when he agreed to buy Express Scripts thirteen months after the Anthem deal died, converting Cigna from an insurer into the second largest pharmacy benefit manager.

s: Biohaven Pharmaceutical DEFM14A filed 30 August 2022 (Pfizer merger at 148.50 dollars cash per share) and Biohaven Ltd DEF 14A filed 13 March 2026 (age 55); BHVN close 13.85 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Merger proxy: 1,921,066 shares beneficially owned, of which 922,941 were held outright through direct, 401k and two family trusts. 922,941 x 148.50 = 137.1 million dollars cash in October 2022, plus vested option proceeds, plus 3,849,354 Biohaven Ltd shares today x 13.85 = 53.3 million; taxed and netted to 0.22.
did: Left Bristol Myers Squibb neuroscience to co-found Biohaven in New Haven in 2013, licensed the failed ALS compound rimegepant family from Bristol Myers, ran it through migraine trials and launched Nurtec ODT in 2020; Pfizer bought the company for 11.6 billion dollars in cash in October 2022 at 148.50 dollars a share.
why: Big pharma had shelved oral CGRP inhibitors after liver toxicity killed an earlier generation, so the chemistry was cheap to in-license. Biohaven bought derisked molecules, spent its money on trials rather than discovery, and won a label allowing both acute and preventive use that no rival had.
obst: Biohaven had to fund late stage migraine trials against companies a hundred times its size, financing them with royalty and debt deals from Royalty Pharma rather than dilution, and then launch Nurtec into a market where Allergan had a two year head start and a far larger sales force.
turn: The 2018 pivotal rimegepant readouts, which showed both acute and preventive benefit and triggered the Pfizer collaboration that became the 2022 cash takeout.

s: The Chefs Warehouse DEF 14A filed 25 March 2026 (ownership as of 16 March 2026, age 62); CHEF close 110.61 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Proxy beneficial ownership table: 1,313,264 shares, 3.2 percent of class, including 400,000 held through a grantor retained annuity trust. 1,313,264 x 110.61 = 145.3 million dollars.
did: Co-founded the specialty food distributor with his brother Christopher in 1985 as Dairyland USA, running the warehouses and delivery network supplying independent chefs in Manhattan and later 30 metro markets; vice chairman since the 2011 listing and chief operating officer since 2022.
why: Broadline distributors make money on pallet volume and cannot profitably deliver 40 cases of imported cheese to a 60 seat restaurant at 6am. Chefs Warehouse built dense urban routes carrying tens of thousands of hard to source items the chef, not a purchasing manager, chooses.
obst: Independent restaurants, their entire customer base, shut in March 2020; revenue fell by roughly a third for the year and the company had to raise convertible notes and equity at depressed prices to survive a market where its competitors had grocery channels to fall back on.
turn: The July 2011 initial public offering, which gave the brothers acquisition currency to roll up regional specialty distributors from Los Angeles to Miami.

s: Schedule 13G/A filed by R. Philip Silver 30 January 2026 and Silgan Holdings DEF 14A filed 16 April 2026 (age 72 in the 2015 proxy); SLGN close 42.39 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Own Schedule 13G/A: 8,935,545 shares, 8.46 percent of Silgan, being 61,411 held directly and 8,874,134 in a family revocable trust he controls. 8,935,545 x 42.39 = 378.8 million dollars. His SEC address of record is the Silgan office in Norwalk, Connecticut.
did: Former president of Continental Can who, with Greg Horrigan, founded Silgan in 1987 to buy the captive can plants food companies wanted off their books, starting with Nestle Carnation, then bought American National Can food cans in 1995 and took the company public in 1997; Silgan now makes most US metal food cans.
why: A steel food can is mostly air, so it cannot travel far and the plant must sit beside the cannery. Buying captive plants with long supply contracts attached meant Silgan inherited the customer with the asset, and consolidation from five suppliers to two brought contractual cost pass through.
obst: The 1987 launch was financed with debt against plants whose only customer was the food company that had just sold them; a single insourcing decision by Nestle Carnation or Del Monte could have wiped out the equity, so they signed multi year supply agreements before closing each deal.
turn: The August 1995 purchase of American National Can metal food can business, which roughly doubled Silgan and made it the largest food can maker in the United States.

s: Schedule 13G/A filed by D. Greg Horrigan 9 May 2025 and Silgan Holdings DEF 14A filed 16 April 2026 (6.66 percent; age 71 in the 2015 proxy); SLGN close 42.39 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Own Schedule 13G/A: 7,043,303 shares, 6.66 percent of Silgan, of which 26,813 held directly and the balance in family trusts. 7,043,303 x 42.39 = 298.6 million dollars. SEC address of record is 4 Landmark Square, Stamford, Connecticut.
did: Was executive vice president and operating officer of Continental Can when he and Philip Silver founded Silgan in 1987; ran the plants and the labour side while Silver ran the deals, serving as co-chief executive until 2006 and a director until 2023, and still holds 6.7 percent of the company.
why: Silgan ran acquired plants at higher line speeds and lower scrap than the food companies had, so each purchase paid for itself out of operating improvement rather than synergy promises. Owning plastics and closures too let it bid on a customer entire packaging spend.
obst: The company was built inside a declining category: US metal food can volumes have fallen for three decades as consumers moved to fresh and frozen, so growth had to come from taking plants and share from rivals while holding margins in a shrinking market.
turn: The February 1997 initial public offering, which refinanced the leveraged buyout debt and converted two founders equity in a private roll up into liquid, still concentrated public stock.

s: Amphenol Corporation DEF 14A filed 8 April 2026 (ownership as of 23 March 2026, age 56); APH close 157.01 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Proxy: 460,000 shares owned plus 2,173,159 exercisable options. Option table strikes are 21.99, 22.37, 22.55, 33.30, 33.80, 37.90 and 65.96 dollars on 2,013,054 vested options, giving about 262 million dollars of intrinsic value at 157.01; shares add 72.2 million. Netted for exercise tax to about 0.3.
did: Joined Amphenol from Deloitte in 2004 as controller and has been chief financial officer since 2015, adding executive vice president in 2026; over that stretch revenue went from about 5.6 billion to more than 20 billion dollars as Amphenol high speed interconnects became a gating part for AI server racks.
why: Amphenol pays officers almost entirely in ten year options struck at the money and grants them every May, so a decade of 20 percent compounding turns a finance executive grant stack into nine figures. Underneath sits decentralised general managers plus continuous bolt on acquisitions funded from cash flow.
obst: Amphenol earnings stalled from 2018 to 2020 as the trade war taxed its China heavy manufacturing base and the mobile device cycle rolled over; the company had to shift capacity and capital into datacenter, defence and automotive before the interconnect boom arrived.
turn: The 2023 to 2025 AI datacenter buildout, when high speed backplane and power interconnects became scarce and Amphenol market value tripled past 190 billion dollars.

s: EMCOR Group DEF 14A filed 21 April 2026 (age 61, ownership table); EME close 776.62 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: Proxy beneficial ownership: 170,299 shares x 776.62 = 132.3 million dollars. Proxy also shows 20,995 shares vesting in 2025 alone worth 9.9 million, and comparable vesting each year since 2011, so accumulated after tax proceeds are added to reach 0.2.
did: Left Carrier to join EMCOR as president in 2004 and became chief executive in 2011; grew the mechanical and electrical contractor from about 5 billion to more than 16 billion dollars of revenue, shifted the mix toward recurring building services, and retired roughly a third of the shares.
why: EMCOR sells scarce skilled labour, not equipment: when hyperscalers need gigawatts of datacenter capacity the constraint is having thousands of electricians and pipefitters already trained and on payroll. That workforce cannot be conjured, so EMCOR picks jobs on margin instead of bidding for volume.
obst: US non residential construction collapsed from 2009 to 2012 just as he was taking over; he consolidated and closed subsidiaries and pushed into maintenance and service contracts rather than bid work at negative margins to keep crews busy.
turn: The 2021 to 2025 datacenter and semiconductor fabrication wave, when EMCOR remaining backlog capacity became the binding constraint and margins roughly doubled.

s: WWE DEF 14A filed 7 April 2023 (ownership as of 15 March 2023) and the September 2023 WWE Endeavor merger, one TKO share per WWE share; TKO close 193.14 dollars, 21 August 2026
m: WWE proxy: 1,940,190 shares, being 90,797 Class A held directly and 1,849,393 Class B in the 2008 Vincent McMahon irrevocable trust over which she has sole dispositive power. Converted one for one into TKO, 1,940,190 x 193.14 = 374.7 million dollars; marked to 0.37 for possible post 2023 sales.
did: Joined WWE in 1998, ran creative from 2002, was chief brand officer from 2013 and became interim then co-chief executive in 2022 after her father resigned over hush money payments, steering the company through the year it agreed to merge with UFC into TKO; her stake sits in a 2008 family trust.
why: WWE value was unlocked when the 2018 and 2019 Fox and USA renewals repriced wrestling as live sports inventory at roughly 470 million dollars a year. Because the family held super voting Class B shares placed in trust in 2008, a small economic stake controlled the company later sold to Endeavor.
obst: She took the top job in June 2022 in the middle of a federal investigation and board inquiry into her father undisclosed payments, ran the company for six months, and then had him force his way back onto the board in January 2023 to push a sale; she resigned two weeks later.
turn: The April 2023 agreement to merge WWE with Endeavor UFC into TKO, which converted the family control stake into liquid shares of a 36 billion dollar sports company.
